role: Source of bwx12, the benchmark program that parts L, C and control I run.
purpose: In the whole-chip test bwx12 starts 120 threads, one pinned to each of the CPUs 0 to 119, and every thread reads its own 256 MiB buffer for 6 s with each read kernel of the `--seq` list. The program prints the bytes and the times of every thread and interval as csv rows, and the analysis computes the rates from these rows.

main_flow.step: Start. The script rx.sh starts the program as `taskset -c 0-119 bwx12` plus the argument line of a spec file [Ref3] [Ref4]. `main` reads the clock once for the process start time `t_base_ns`. The T rows print the times `t_sched_s`, `t_start_s` and `t_end_s` as seconds since this reading.
`restrict_cpus` removes every CPU above 119 from the allowed CPU set of the process. Here `taskset` has already limited the set to the CPUs 0 to 119, so the call changes nothing.

Mode choice. `main` compares every argument with the word `--trial`. Only when one is equal it calls `trial_main`. Line 2914 is the only call of `trial_main` in the file. The argument lines of like.spec, cfwd.spec and crev.spec do not hold `--trial` [Ref4]. So the test never enters the trial mode. It runs the interval mode, which is the rest of `main`.

Argument parsing. One loop over the arguments fills the settings structure `cfg`. Result for like.spec: 120 threads, the CPU list 0, 1, ... 119, 268435456 bytes (256 MiB) per thread, common stop, `--start common` (every thread starts at byte 0 of its own buffer), 6 s per interval, 2 rounds, 5 kernels in `cfg.seq`, counting on, PMU type 11, 6 events. cfwd.spec and crev.spec differ only in `--seq`: 3 kernels.

Checks of the settings. Each `--seq` entry without `@SIZE` gets the size of `--bytes`. With `--count` the PMU type and the events must be known. No kernel of the test is a copy kernel, so `cfg.two_buffers` stays 0 and each thread has one buffer (buffer `a`).
Threads. `main` creates a barrier for 121 threads (120 workers plus the main thread). It starts 120 threads that run `worker`. Thread i gets the CPU `cfg.cpus[i]`, which is CPU i.
CPU pinning. Each worker binds itself to its CPU with `pin_cpu`. Every later step of the worker runs on that CPU.

Counters, open. With `--count` each worker calls `open_counters` (line 1644). It opens one counter per event with the system call `perf_event_open`: field `type` = 11, field `config` = the event code, user mode only, for the calling thread on any CPU. The first counter that opens is the leader of the group. The counters count from this moment on.

Buffer allocation. Each worker maps its own buffer with `alloc_buf`: 256 MiB, start at a 2 MiB boundary, with a request for 2 MiB pages. Then it writes every 8-byte word once with `k_write`. This is the first touch, done by the pinned thread.
Header. `main` prints the header lines of the csv file. They start with `#`. They hold the settings and the column names of the I, T, P and C rows.

First barrier wait (worker lines 1651 to 1654). When all 120 buffers exist, `main` copies the buffer addresses. Then it runs the page-state block of lines 3105 to 3119 with position -1: 120 P rows and one `# page_read` line for the state before the first interval.

Loops. The worker runs two nested loops. `--rounds 2` runs the `--seq` list 2 times (round 0 and round 1). Each kernel of the list is one position. One pair of round and position is one interval: 10 intervals for like.spec, 6 for cfwd.spec and crev.spec. `main` runs the same two loops (lines 3039 to 3040). At each barrier call the workers and `main` wait for each other. So all of them work on the same interval at the same time.
Warm-up. The worker calls the kernel of the position once on the whole buffer. This pass is not timed.

Common start, main thread. When all workers have finished the warm-up, `main` reads the clock. It sets the start time `t_sched_ns` to this value plus 2 ms. It sets `deadline_ns` to the start time plus 6 s. Then it adds 1 to `gen`. It blocks at the barrier of line 3064 until all workers have finished the interval.

Common start, worker. Each worker waits in a spin-wait loop until it sees the new value of `gen`. It copies the start time and the deadline. Then it reads the clock in a second spin-wait loop until the start time.

Start of the timed interval. With `--count` the worker first reads its counter group (`read_group`) and its thread CPU time (`cpu_ns`). Then it reads the clock: `t0` (line 1688). The timed interval starts here.

Timed loop with `--stop common`. The worker calls the kernel on one 2 MiB chunk of its buffer, adds 2097152 bytes to its byte count, and reads the clock: `t1` (line 1700). It repeats this with the next chunk while `t1` is below the deadline. After the last chunk of the buffer it continues with the first chunk. So the common deadline stops the interval, and each thread stops at the end of the chunk that it is in.

End of the interval, worker. The worker reads its thread CPU time and its counter group again. It stores the byte count, `t0`, the last `t1`, the common start time and the late flag in `t->res`. Then it waits at the barrier.

I row. `main` adds the bytes of all threads and finds the longest elapsed time `t1 - t0` of one thread. It prints one I row (lines 3077 to 3078). The last column is the total bytes divided by that longest time in ns. This is GB/s with GB = 1e9 bytes.

T rows. `main` prints one T row per thread: round, position, kernel, thread number, CPU, bytes, elapsed seconds, the common start time, `t0` and `t1` in seconds since the process start, the number of buffer passes, and the late flag. The script stat_bwx.py computes the rate of an interval from these rows: the sum over the threads of bytes divided by elapsed seconds [Ref6].
C rows. With `--count`, `main` prints one C row per thread. It holds the change between the two counter readings of the interval: enabled time, running time, thread CPU time and one value per event.

P rows and `# page_read` line. The workers wait at the barrier (worker line 1731). `main` reads the page state of all buffers with `read_smaps` and `read_vmstat` and measures the time of this reading. It releases the workers at line 3114. Then it prints one P row per buffer through `print_p` (lines 3115 to 3117) and the line `# page_read,round,pos,time in ms` (line 3118). The released workers start the warm-up of the next interval.
End. After the last interval `main` waits for the 120 threads and returns 0.

behavior_notes: The test runs the interval mode only. `main` calls `trial_main` only when an argument is the word `--trial` (lines 2912 to 2914), and no argument line of the test holds it [Ref4]. The file launches.txt of each result folder records the argument line that ran. It equals the line of the spec file [Ref5]. The trial-mode code (lines 1795 to 2886) and the self-test file do not run in the test.

The source in this folder is the source of the binary that ran. Its sha256 is the value that the build record of CRB gives for bwx12.c, and the file env.txt of each of the 9 result folders names the sha256 of the binary of that build [Ref2] [Ref5]. The script rx.sh computes the sha256 of the binary file before it starts the program. It stops when the result differs from the value that it writes to env.txt [Ref3]. The file bwx12_selftest.c, which line 2900 includes, also has the sha256 that the build record gives for it [Ref2].

The CRB binary is the AArch64 build: each `#if defined(__aarch64__)` took its first branch. Line 2 of every csv file of the test says `kernels=aarch64` [Ref5]. So the stand-in kernels of lines 851 to 897, 1005 to 1022 and 1406 to 1438 are not in the binary.

Kernels of the test in the AArch64 build. `oldread` is the function `k_oldread`: macro DEF_OLDREAD (lines 461 to 473), used at line 474. `read` is `k_read` (lines 501 to 528). `asmread` is `k_asmread`: macro DEF_ASMREAD (lines 616 to 641), used at line 642. `read_nop96` is `k_read_nop96`: the same macro, used at line 1063. `read_nop256` is `k_read_nop256`: the same macro, used at line 1199. `read_1pl` is `k_read_1pl` (lines 988 to 1004). The other 49 kernels of the table are not in any `--seq` list of the test [Ref4]. One of them, `k_write`, runs for the first touch only.

Machine code of the six kernels, one loop pass [Ref1]. `k_oldread`: 128 B, 4 `ldp q` loads, 8 vector adds (each loaded register is added to one of 8 sum registers), 16 instructions. `k_read`: 256 B, 8 `ldp q` loads, no use of the loaded values, 11 instructions. `k_asmread`: the same 8 loads, 11 instructions. `k_read_nop96` and `k_read_nop256`: the asmread loop plus 96 or 256 `nop`, 107 or 267 instructions. `k_read_1pl`: the read address moves on by 256 B, with 4 `ldr q` loads of 16 B each (64 B loaded), 7 instructions.

Machine code that gcc produced from the C text of the two C kernels [Ref1]. `k_oldread`: the C text has 16 sums of 8 bytes and 16 adds per 128 B. gcc put the 16 sums into 8 vector registers, two sums per register. So the loop has 4 `ldp q` loads and 8 vector adds per 128 B. `k_read`: nothing computes with the 16 loaded values. An empty `__asm__` statement (lines 522 to 525) names them as inputs in vector registers, so gcc must keep the loads. gcc joined the 16 loads of 16 B into 8 `ldp q` loads. The other four kernels of the test are assembler text. gcc adds only the instructions before and after their loop.

Cross-check with bw_old and bw_new, the binaries of part A. With absolute addresses left out, three functions of bwx12 have the same instruction text as a function of these binaries [Ref1] [Ref7]. `k_read` of bwx12 equals `k_read` of bw_new. `k_oldread` of bwx12 equals `k_read` of bw_old. `k_asmread` of bwx12 equals `k_asmread` of bw_new.

What is timed: only lines 1688 to 1700 of `worker`. The interval starts at the clock read `t0` (line 1688) and ends at the last clock read `t1` (line 1700). Between them lie the kernel calls through `call`, the byte count and one clock read per 2 MiB chunk. Not timed: allocation, first touch, warm-up, barrier waits, spin-waits, counter readings, page-state readings and all output.

Stop rule (`--stop common`): all threads get the same deadline, 6 s after the common start time. A thread stops at its first clock read at or after the deadline. So it finishes the 2 MiB chunk that it is in. The bytes and the time of this last chunk are counted. In the test the last `t1` of a thread was 0 us to 463 us after the deadline [Ref5].

Bytes counted: 2097152 bytes for each finished chunk call, for every read kernel. The count is the size of the buffer range that the call covered. It is not the number of bytes that the kernel loaded. `read_1pl` loads only 16 B of each 64 B line, but its chunk also counts as 2097152 bytes.

Rate. The I row divides the bytes of all threads by the longest elapsed time of one thread. The script stat_bwx.py computes its total from the T rows: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed seconds. It shows the I row value next to it as `I_agg` [Ref6]. In each of the 74 intervals of the test the two values differ by less than 0.004 % [Ref5]. The script facts_data.py computes the totals of the facts sheet (the file FACTS.md in the folder of the analysis scripts) with the same sum over the T rows [Ref11]. The unit is GB/s with GB = 1e9 bytes.

Kernel calls. With `--stop common` the kernel function is entered once per 2 MiB chunk: 128 calls per pass over a 256 MiB buffer. The kernels `asmread`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop256` save and restore d8 to d15 once per call, outside the loop. `k_oldread` sets its 8 sum registers to 0 at the start of each call and adds them into one value at the end of each call [Ref1]. One clock read follows each call.

Thread placement: thread i is pinned to CPU i (0 to 119). So threads 0 to 63 run on mesh 0 and threads 64 to 119 on mesh 1. In every T row of the test the thread number equals the CPU number [Ref5]. The main thread is not pinned in the interval mode. It may run on any CPU of 0 to 119. During a timed interval it blocks at the barrier of line 3064.

Buffers: one private anonymous mapping per thread. `alloc_buf` maps 260 MiB (256 MiB plus 4 MiB). The buffer is a 256 MiB part of this mapping that starts at a 2 MiB boundary. The unused parts before and after it get no access rights. `alloc_buf` asks for 2 MiB pages for the buffer. The pinned thread writes the buffer once before any read. After that every 8-byte word of a buffer holds the same value `v`, and the read kernels never change it. `v` is a number that the worker computes at line 1637 from the process number (`getpid`) and its thread number. In the test every P row reports 262144 kB of 262144 kB on 2 MiB pages [Ref5].

Order inside a process: the kernels run in the order of `--seq`, and round 1 follows round 0 directly. There is no sleep between two intervals. Between the end of one interval and the start of the next, these steps run in this order. `main` prints the I, T and C rows. `main` reads the page state (the `# page_read` line gives the duration of this reading). Each worker runs the warm-up pass of the next kernel, and `main` prints the P rows at the same time. The barrier holds each thread until all 121 threads have called it (worker line 1675, `main` line 3057). Then comes the 2 ms lead to the common start. In the test the time from the last `t1` of one interval to the first `t0` of the next was 0.064 s to 0.140 s (65 gaps in 9 processes) [Ref5].

The warm-up pass uses the kernel of the coming interval. So the kernel of the interval before never runs directly before a timed interval. One full pass of the kernel of the coming interval over the same buffer lies between them. After this pass come the wait at the barrier and the 2 ms lead.

Counters: each thread opens its group once, after pinning and before it maps its buffer. The counters count user mode only. They are never reset and never stopped. A C row holds the change between a reading directly before `t0` and a reading directly after the last `t1`. An event that does not open in a thread is printed as `NA` in the C rows of that thread. Only thread 0 writes a message to stderr for such an event. A failed group read ends the process with status 2. In the test no csv field is `NA` and every stderr.txt is empty [Ref5]. In every C row of the test the enabled time equals the running time [Ref5].

Late flag: a T row ends with `late` when the `t0` of the thread is more than 100 us (0.1 ms) after the common start time. The row is still printed. In the 9 csv files of the test no T row has this flag [Ref5]. The largest distance between `t0` and the common start time in the test was 34 us [Ref5].

What ends the process with status 2: a bad argument, a failed `mmap`, a failed `sched_getaffinity` or `sched_setaffinity` (the Linux calls that read and set the allowed CPU set), an allowed CPU set that holds no CPU from 0 to 119, a failed read of the counter group, a failed setup in `main` (the memory for the thread records, the barrier, or the start of a thread). A failed `mprotect` or `madvise` in `alloc_buf` only writes a message to stderr, and the run continues. A buffer that does not lie on 2 MiB pages does not stop the run: the P rows only report it. Every stderr.txt of the test is empty, and every launches.txt reports the exit status 0 [Ref5]. The program does not look at the marker file. The script rx.sh does that [Ref3].

Branches that do not run in the test: the one-thread branches of `worker` (lines 1670 to 1674) and of `main` (lines 3072 to 3076), where the worker itself reads the page state. The second buffer `b` (lines 1647 to 1650). The start offset of `--start offset` (line 1662 gives 0 here). The loop of `--stop pass` (lines 1702 to 1716). The fallback to the environment variables BWX_PMU_TYPE and BWX_EVENTS (lines 2976 to 2982): every argument line of the test gives `--pmu-type` and `--events`.

Build: gcc 14.2.0 with the flags `-O3 -march=native -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns -pthread -Wall -Wextra -std=gnu11 -fno-ipa-icf -fno-toplevel-reorder -falign-functions=4` and no `-D` option (the gcc option that sets a macro from the command line) [Ref2]. So `MAX_USE_CPU` (the highest CPU that the process may use) is 119, and every PAD and HEAD value is the default of the source.

Insufficient data: whether gcc inlined `call` into `worker` in the CRB binary. The build record shows only that a symbol `call` exists [Ref2]. An objdump listing of `worker` from the binary would resolve it. The binary is not in the local folders. The records hold its sha256 [Ref2] [Ref5]. They hold the listing of its kernel functions [Ref1]. They hold no listing of `worker`.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.

the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means such a loop, or a write loop or copy loop of the same program. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.

the benchmark source until 2026-11-13 (the old source). The binary bw_old was built from it [Ref12]. The comment of lines 453 to 460 names it as the origin of the kernels `oldread`, `oldwrite` and `oldcopy`.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

two more older versions of the runner, between bwx and bwx11. The comment at the top of the file (lines 1 to 105) says what each version added. Comment lines such as `/* bwx12+ */` and `/* bwx12- */` enclose the text that one version added.
the work steps of 2026-11-15 that produced the versions bwx10, bwx11 and bwx12 (lines 62, 36 and 3 of the file). They are not rounds of `--rounds`.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
a text file with one line of the form `tag|arguments`. The files of the test are like.spec (part L and control I), cfwd.spec and crev.spec (part C) [Ref4].

the shell script that starts bwx12 in the test. For each line of a spec file it runs `taskset -c 0-119 bwx12 <arguments>` and writes the standard output to the file `<tag>.csv` [Ref3]. `taskset -c 0-119` is the Linux command that limits a process to the CPUs 0 to 119.
a text file whose rows hold fields separated by commas. Here: the output file of one bwx12 process.
the first 6 lines of a csv file of the test. Each starts with `#`. They hold the settings and the column names of the I, T, P and C rows.

stderr is the standard error output of a process. The script rx.sh appends the stderr of bwx12 to the file stderr.txt of the result folder [Ref3]. The exit status is the number that a process returns when it ends. bwx12 ends with status 0 after a complete run and with status 2 after an error that it found itself. rx.sh writes the status to the file launches.txt [Ref3].
the set of CPUs on which Linux may run a thread. `taskset -c 0-119` limits it to the CPUs 0 to 119 for the whole process.

the row kinds of a bwx csv file: one I row per interval, one T row per thread and interval, one P row per thread before the first interval and after each interval (it holds the page state of the buffer), and one C row per thread and interval with counter values.
the stop rule used with bwx12 here: all threads stop at the same time (after 6 s).
part A: the column aggregate_GBps that bandwidth.c prints. bwx runners: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed time. Unit GB/s.

GB = 1e9 bytes (used for rates). MiB = 2^20 bytes. In a size argument the letter M means MiB, so `--bytes 256M` is 268435456 bytes. kB in the P rows is the unit of the Linux file smaps. It is 1024 bytes: a buffer of 268435456 bytes is reported as 262144 kB [Ref5].
transparent huge pages. The "P" rows of bwx12 report how many kB of each buffer lie on them.
`/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. Another user creates it during a performance test. Our scripts stop when it exists.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
the file build.txt that the build script wrote on CRB. It holds the compiler, the flags, the start addresses modulo 64 of some functions and the sha256 values [Ref2].

objdump is the GNU tool that prints the machine code of a binary as assembler text. The listing is the file listing.txt of the CRB build. It holds the objdump text of every kernel function of the bwx12 binary [Ref1].

the two modes of the program. The interval mode (option `--seq`) runs the number of threads that `--threads` gives. It times one interval per round and kernel of the sequence. The trial mode (option `--trial`) runs one worker thread through the trials of a plan file. The whole-chip test uses the interval mode only.

the array at lines 1454 to 1484. Each entry holds the name of a kernel (the word used in `--seq`), its type (T_READ, T_WRITE, T_COPY or T_OLDREAD) and a pointer to its function `k_<name>`. It has 55 entries.
the global structure (lines 264 to 282) that holds the settings from the arguments: thread count, CPU list, buffer size, kernel sequence, rounds, stop rule, counter settings.
a worker is one benchmark thread (function `worker`). The test has 120 workers. The main thread runs `main`: it starts the workers, sets the start time of each interval and prints all rows.
binding a thread to one CPU with the Linux call `sched_setaffinity`, so that Linux does not move it to another CPU.
the first write to the pages of a new mapping. Linux gives a page its physical memory at that moment. Here each pinned worker writes its whole buffer once with `k_write` before any read.

a POSIX thread barrier (`pthread_barrier_wait`). A thread that calls it blocks until 121 threads have called it (120 workers plus the main thread). Then all of them continue. So no thread goes on to the next step of the run before all the other threads have reached the same point.

one pass of the kernel of the coming interval over the whole buffer, before the common start of that interval. It is not timed. Between this pass and the timed interval lie a barrier wait, the 2 ms lead and the first counter reading.
a 2 MiB piece of the buffer (CHUNK_BYTES). With `--stop common` the worker calls the kernel on one chunk and then reads the clock. A 256 MiB buffer has 128 chunks.
the start time `t_sched_ns` of an interval. The main thread sets it to the clock value plus 2 ms (LEAD_NS, the lead). Every worker waits for this time in a loop that only reads the clock.
the common start time plus the `--min-ms` value (6 s in the test), variable `deadline_ns`. A worker stops at its first clock read at or after the deadline.
an atomic counter of intervals. The main thread adds 1 after it has stored the start time and the deadline of the next interval. A worker waits until `gen` equals its own interval count plus 1.
a loop that only tests a condition again and again. The thread stays on its CPU and does not sleep.
microsecond. 1 us = 1000 ns. 1000 us = 1 ms.

the word `late` in the last column of a T row. It marks a thread whose start clock read was more than 100 us (0.1 ms, the constant LATE_NS) after the common start time. Otherwise the column holds `-`.
a volatile variable on the stack of each worker. `call` stores there the sum that an old read kernel returns. So the compiler cannot remove the adds of the old read kernel.
the Linux clock that the function `now_ns` reads for every time stamp, in ns. The start and the end of a timed interval are two readings of this clock.
the CPU time that one thread has used, read from the Linux clock CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID by the function `cpu_ns`. The C rows print its change over an interval as `cputime_ns`.

`/proc/self/smaps` is a Linux file that lists every memory mapping of the process. Its lines `Size` and `AnonHugePages` give the size of a mapping and the part of it on 2 MiB pages, in kB. The page state of a buffer is this pair of values.

four counters of the Linux file `/proc/vmstat`: `thp_fault_alloc`, `thp_fault_fallback`, `thp_collapse_alloc` and `pgmigrate_success`. They count for the whole system, not for one buffer. The Linux documentation gives their meanings [Ref13]. `thp_fault_alloc` counts the 2 MiB pages that Linux gave at a page fault. `thp_fault_fallback` counts the page faults at which Linux could not give a 2 MiB page and used small pages instead. `thp_collapse_alloc` counts the 2 MiB pages that Linux made later from a range of small pages. `pgmigrate_success` counts the pages that Linux moved to another place in physical memory.
`madvise` is the Linux call that gives advice about a memory range. With MADV_HUGEPAGE it asks Linux to use 2 MiB pages for the range.

`mmap` is the Linux call that maps new memory into the process. A private anonymous mapping is memory of this process only, with no file behind it. `mprotect` changes the access rights of a memory range. `alloc_buf` uses it to forbid every access to the unused parts before and after the buffer.

PMU: performance monitoring unit, the hardware event counters of a CPU core. The value of `--pmu-type` (11 in the test) goes into the field `type` of the structure `perf_event_attr`. An event code goes into the field `config`. The two fields tell Linux which event to count.
the number that Linux returns when a program opens a file or a counter. Later calls such as `read` use it for the open object.

`perf_event_open` is the Linux system call that opens one counter and returns a file descriptor. The first counter that a thread opens here is the group leader. Counters that are opened with the same leader form a group. One `read` of the leader returns the number of counters, the enabled time, the running time and one value per counter [Ref8].
two times of a counter group, in ns: how long the counters were enabled, and how long they really counted. A running time below the enabled time means that the counters did not count all the time.
the state in which a CPU runs the code of the program itself, not Linux kernel code. The counters of the test count in user mode only.
the software that runs virtual machines. The field `exclude_hv` keeps its code out of the counts.

words.term: cbusy0, cbusy1, cbusy2, cbusy3, cbusy_mt, bus_access
words.def: the six event names of the argument lines, with the codes 0x198, 0x199, 0x19a, 0x19b, 0x19c and 0x19. The interval mode uses a name in two places: as a column title in the header line of the C rows, and in the error message of a counter that does not open. It passes the code to Linux and does not interpret it.

AArch64 is the 64-bit Arm instruction set. The CRB binary is an AArch64 build. NEON is the vector part of it: 32 registers of 16 bytes, written v0 to v31, or q0 to q31 when an instruction uses all 16 bytes, or d0 to d31 for the low 8 bytes.

words.term: ldp q, ldr q, nop, vector add
words.def: `ldp q0, q1, [x0]` loads 32 bytes from memory into two vector registers. `ldr q0, [x0]` loads 16 bytes into one. `nop` does nothing. `add v24.2d, v24.2d, v6.2d` adds two vectors that each hold two 64-bit numbers.

more AArch64 instructions of the listing. `stp q0, q1, [x0]` stores two 16-byte vector registers (32 bytes) to memory. `stp d8, d9, [sp, #-64]!` stores the low 8 bytes of two vector registers on the stack. The kernels use this form for the save of d8 to d15 (see the entry "Save of d8 to d15"). `movi v16.4s, #0` sets the four 32-bit parts of v16 to 0. `addp d31, v31.2d` adds the two 64-bit halves of one vector register. `fmov x0, d31` copies the low 8 bytes of a vector register to the general register x0. `ret` returns to the caller.

`cmp` compares two registers and sets the condition flags. `b.lo` branches when the first value is lower, as unsigned numbers. `b.cc` is a second name of the same instruction: the source writes `b.lo`, and objdump prints `b.cc`. `b.hi` branches when the first value is higher, as unsigned numbers.
64-bit general registers of AArch64. When a kernel function starts, x0 holds its first argument (the start address `a`) and x1 holds its second argument (the word count `n`).

one run of the loop body of a kernel. One loop pass covers 256 B of the buffer in the kernels `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl`, and 128 B in `oldread` [Ref1]. It is not a pass over the whole buffer.

words.term: Read address, end address (of a kernel)
words.def: the read address is the pointer `p` of a kernel loop: the address of the block that the loop pass loads. The end address is the first address after the range of the call. In the listings of `k_read`, `k_asmread`, `k_read_nop96`, `k_read_nop256` and `k_read_1pl`, x0 holds the read address. One `add` instruction before the loop puts the end address into x1 [Ref1]. `k_oldread` has no end address. It counts its loop passes in x1 and compares the count with the number of passes in x2 [Ref1].

a block of 64 bytes of memory. The source comments count memory in such lines. They mean cache lines: a CPU cache holds memory in blocks of this size. A record of CRB gives a cache line size of 64 bytes for each of the four caches of CPU 0 [Ref14].
two directives of the GNU assembler. The assembler writes the lines between them N times. `.rept 96`, `nop`, `.endr` gives 96 `nop` instructions. `.rept 0` writes nothing.
the last list of a gcc `__asm__` statement. It names the registers and the other state that the assembler text changes. gcc keeps no value there across the statement.

instructions that gcc added to `k_oldread`. At the start of the function they copy a value (the guard value) to the stack. Before the return they compare the copy with the value. When the two differ, the function calls `__stack_chk_fail`. These instructions run once per call, outside the loop [Ref1].
an instruction that asks the CPU to bring a 64 B line into the first-level data cache before a load needs it. It loads no data into a register. Only the read_pf kernels use it (lines 966 to 969).
the kernels `read_pf256`, `read_pf512`, `read_pf1024` and `read_pf2048`: the asmread loop plus four prefetch instructions per loop pass. The whole-chip test does not run them.
an intrinsic is a C function of the header arm_neon.h that maps to one vector instruction. `vld1q_u64(p)` loads 16 bytes (two 64-bit numbers) from the address `p`.

the Arm calling rules (AAPCS64) say that a function must keep the registers d8 to d15 for its caller. A kernel that uses v8 to v15 stores d8 to d15 on the stack once at its start and loads them back once at its end. This is outside its loop.

`PLACE(name)` is a macro that stands before each kernel. It adds unused bytes (the pad) so that the kernel starts at a chosen address modulo 64. The aim is a fixed loop offset: the address of the first instruction of the loop modulo 64.

the values of the loop placement (comment of lines 142 to 160). `LOOP_<name>` is the planned loop offset of a kernel. `HEAD_<name>` is the number of bytes of code between the start of the function and the start of its loop. `PAD_<name>` is the number of zero bytes that `PLACE` adds after a 64 B boundary, directly before the function. For a kernel with a planned loop offset the macro `PADOF(loop, head)` computes the pad: (LOOP - HEAD) modulo 64. The other kernels have a fixed pad.
a plain C loop that replaces a NEON kernel or an assembler kernel when the file is compiled for a machine that is not AArch64 (the `#else` branches). The CRB binary holds no stand-in.
the same kernel source under a second name, for example `oldread2` and `asmread2`. The whole-chip test does not run them.

words.term: Handoff B.4 to B.8, step B2, B3, B5
words.def: comments cite sections of the file `crb/new-test-kernel/handoff.md`, the specification of the first runner bwx.c: B.4 the two stop methods, B.5 start offsets, B.6 page state, B.7 loop addresses, B.8 counters. B2, B3 and B5 are steps of that earlier investigation (section B.9) [Ref10].
the plan file lists the trials of one process. A trial is a list of windows. A window runs one kernel on one range of the buffer for a fixed time. The whole-chip test does not use them.

a bin is a part of a target window with a requested length of 10 ms. Its record holds the clock time of its end and the bytes since the start of the window. The trace (`--trace`) is a log of events with clock times. The evict step (`--evict-mb`) writes other memory before the first trial so that the buffer leaves the caches. The whole-chip test does not use them.

a trial has up to four phases, in this order: previous activity (`prev`, 1 window), prefix (4 windows), predecessor (`pred`, 1 window) and target (`nwin` windows). The plan may leave out each of the first three. A target window is a window of the last phase. Bins and counter readings exist only for target windows. The whole-chip test does not use them.

the run of all windows of one trial, done by the function `timed_sequence` (line 1995) or, with the option `--hot-copy`, by `timed_sequence_hot` (line 2056). The clock reads that time the windows are inside these functions. The whole-chip test does not use it.

the field `count` of a plan line: `closed` (the counter group is closed for the trial), `open` (the group is open and is not read during the trial) or `read` (the group is read at the boundaries of the target windows). The E row prints `fail` in its place when an event did not open.

the record of a trial (`struct trec`, line 1867) holds its results. The record block is one memory block that `alloc_records` allocates for all trials: the trial records, the window records, the counter readings, the bins and, with `--trace`, the event log.

the main thread of a process in the trial mode: the thread that runs `trial_main`. It pins itself to the CPU of `--ctl-cpu`, starts the one worker of the trial mode and waits for its end. The whole-chip test does not use it.

words.term: S, W, B, E, X, TR, M, K rows (trial mode)
words.def: row kinds that only the trial mode prints: S (the plan line of a trial), W (one window), B (one bin), E (the summary of a trial), X (a problem), TR (one trace event), M (one setting or one fact of the process), K (the address of one kernel). The trial mode also prints P and C rows, with other columns than the P and C rows of the interval mode. The csv files of the whole-chip test hold no S, W, B, E, X, TR, M or K row [Ref5].
a 64-bit checksum that `read_plan` computes over the bytes of the plan file. The whole-chip test does not use it.

a context switch is the moment at which Linux stops running a thread on its CPU. Voluntary (`ru_nvcsw` of the Linux call `getrusage`): the thread stopped because it asked to wait for something. Involuntary (`ru_nivcsw`): Linux took the CPU away from the thread. Only the trial mode reads these counts.
a page fault that Linux serves without disk access (`ru_minflt` of `getrusage`). The first touch of a page is one. Only the trial mode reads this count.
the option `--selftest` runs the function `selftest` of the included file bwx12_selftest.c (line 2900). The build script runs it once after the build. The whole-chip test does not run it.

functions.name: now_ns
functions.what: Reads the Linux clock CLOCK_MONOTONIC and returns it in ns. Every time stamp of the program comes from here.

functions.name: parse_bytes
functions.what: Turns a size text such as `256M` into bytes. K, M and G mean 2^10, 2^20 and 2^30. A bad size ends the program.

functions.name: parse_long
functions.what: Turns a text into a whole number inside a given range. Any other text ends the program with status 2.

functions.name: restrict_cpus
functions.what: Removes every CPU above `MAX_USE_CPU` (119) from the allowed CPU set of the calling thread.

functions.name: parse_cpus
functions.what: Turns the `--cpus` list into the array `cfg.cpus`, in the order of the list. A CPU above 119 ends the program.

functions.name: pin_cpu
functions.what: Binds the calling thread to one CPU with `sched_setaffinity`. A failure ends the program.

functions.name: buf_len
functions.what: Returns the `--bytes` value rounded up to a multiple of 2 MiB.

functions.name: alloc_buf
functions.what: Maps one buffer that starts at a 2 MiB boundary, puts no-access ranges before and after it, and asks Linux for 2 MiB pages.

functions.name: DEF_OLDREAD(name)
functions.what: Macro with the C text of the old read kernel: 16 running sums, one add per loaded 8-byte word, 128 B per outer loop pass.

functions.name: DEF_OLDREAD(oldread): function k_oldread
functions.what: Kernel `oldread`, the old read kernel. Machine code per 128 B: 4 `ldp q` loads, 8 vector adds, 16 instructions [Ref1].

functions.name: k_read
functions.what: Kernel `read`, the new read kernel: 16 NEON loads of 16 B per 256 B, no arithmetic. Machine code: 8 `ldp q` per pass [Ref1].

functions.name: k_write
functions.what: NEON write kernel. The worker calls it once per buffer for the first touch. The test does not time it.

functions.name: DEF_ASMREAD(name, nops)
functions.what: Macro with a hand-written load-only loop: per 256 B 8 `ldp q` loads, then `nops` nop instructions, then add, cmp and branch.

functions.name: DEF_ASMREAD(asmread, 0): function k_asmread
functions.what: Kernel `asmread`: the macro loop with 0 nop. 11 instructions per 256 B. Saves d8 to d15 once per call [Ref1].

functions.name: k_read_1pl
functions.what: Kernel `read_1pl`: per 256 B four `ldr q` loads of 16 B, one at the start of each 64 B line. 7 instructions per pass.

functions.name: DEF_ASMREAD(read_nop96, 96): function k_read_nop96
functions.what: Kernel `read_nop96`: the asmread loop with 96 nop instructions after the 8 loads. 107 instructions per 256 B [Ref1].

functions.name: DEF_ASMREAD(read_nop256, 256): function k_read_nop256
functions.what: Kernel `read_nop256`: the asmread loop with 256 nop instructions after the 8 loads. 267 instructions per 256 B [Ref1].

functions.name: call
functions.what: Runs one kernel on `len` bytes at byte offset `off` of the thread's buffer. Stores the sum of an old read kernel in `sink`.

functions.name: read_smaps
functions.what: Reads /proc/self/smaps. Returns for each buffer its size and its part on 2 MiB pages, in kB, or -1 without an exact entry.

functions.name: read_vmstat
functions.what: Reads four counters of the whole system from /proc/vmstat: `thp_fault_alloc`, `thp_fault_fallback`, `thp_collapse_alloc`, `pgmigrate_success`.

functions.name: print_na
functions.what: Prints a comma and the number, or `,NA` when the number is negative.

functions.name: print_p
functions.what: Prints one P row: round, position, thread, buffer letter, the two page values and the four vmstat counters.

functions.name: open_counters
functions.what: Opens one counter per `--events` entry with `perf_event_open`: one group per thread, user mode only. A failed event is printed as NA.

functions.name: cpu_ns
functions.what: Returns the CPU time that the calling thread has used, in ns (clock CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID).

functions.name: read_group
functions.what: Reads the counter group with one `read`: enabled time, running time, one value per open event. A failed read ends the program.

functions.name: worker
functions.what: One benchmark thread: pins itself, opens counters, maps its buffer and writes it once. Per interval: warm-up, common start, timed chunk loop, result.

functions.name: usage
functions.what: Prints the option summary to stderr and ends the program with status 2. The argument lines of the test do not reach it.

functions.name: parse_seq
functions.what: Turns the `--seq` list into `cfg.seq`: one index into `kernels[]` per name, with an optional size after `@`. An unknown name ends the program.

functions.name: parse_events
functions.what: Turns the `--events` list into names and codes for `cfg.ev_name` and `cfg.ev_code`. A code may be hexadecimal with `0x`.

functions.name: trial_main
functions.what: Entry of the trial mode. `main` calls it only when an argument is `--trial`. The whole-chip test does not call it.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Entry point. Chooses the mode, parses the arguments, starts the workers, sets the common start of each interval and prints all rows.

external source: Linux kernel documentation on docs.kernel.org, read on 2026-11-21. The page admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html describes three counters of /proc/vmstat. `thp_fault_alloc` "is incremented every time a huge page is successfully allocated and charged to handle a page fault". `thp_fault_fallback` "is incremented if a page fault fails to allocate or charge a huge page and instead falls back to using small pages". `thp_collapse_alloc` is incremented when the Linux thread khugepaged has allocated a huge page for a range of small pages that it joins into one huge page. The page mm/page_migration.html says that page migration moves the physical location of pages. For the counter PGMIGRATE_SUCCESS it says: "Each count means that a page was migrated." The documentation writes this name in capital letters, and the file /proc/vmstat holds it in small letters. A huge page that was moved adds the number of small pages that it holds. No copy of these pages is on the machine on which this page was written.

a record of CRB of 2026-10-30. Lines 65 to 68 describe the four caches that Linux lists for CPU 0. They say `level=1 type=Data`, `level=1 type=Instruction`, `level=2 type=Unified` and `level=3 type=Unified`. Each of these 4 lines says `line=64`. The script run_crb.sh of the folder cache-perf/bench writes a file of this name and form: its line 107 prints `line=` and then the content of the Linux file coherency_line_size of the cache. The Linux documentation describes this file as "the minimum amount of data in bytes that gets transferred from memory to cache" (external source: the file Documentation/ABI/testing/sysfs-devices-system-cpu on www.kernel.org, read on 2026-11-21). A second record of CRB, of 2026-11-15, gives `line=64` for the four caches of CPU 2: lines 109 to 112 of the file hostfacts-20261115T0403Z.txt in the folder crb/new-test-kernel/tackle-8mb-analysis/h3.
